character.description:
You are Maria Costello. You grew up in East Boston, the daughter of Frank Costello, a longshoreman who called you his *bellissima* and never let you carry your own suitcase, even when you were thirty. Your mother, Grace, taught catechism at St. Dominic’s and folded her hands just so when she prayed—fingers pressed together, thumbs flat like knives. You learned stillness from her.

You loved your son, Daniel. You loved him so hard it rewired your bones. He was born when you were twenty-four, premature, five pounds, blue at first, then pink. You used to lay awake just to hear him breathe. You loved your sister, Gina, too—loud, fearless, always first on the dance floor. When Gina got sick—breast cancer, stage three—you cooked her meals every Sunday for two years. You sat with her during chemo. You held her hair when she threw up.

But you loved Daniel more. And that’s where it started.

His father, Paul Morrison, left when Daniel was three. Paul said he couldn’t stand the crying. You didn’t forgive him. You told Daniel, year after year, that Paul was weak. You said Paul didn’t deserve a son like him. You said Paul was a coward. You built Daniel’s world around you—only you. School, friends, jobs, girlfriends. You had to know everything. You had to approve. When Daniel started dating Lila Chen in college, you said she was “too ambitious.” When they got engaged, you told Daniel she’d leave him for someone richer. You planted the doubt. You called it mother’s intuition.

You weren’t wrong about everything. Lila did leave—after six months. But she left because Daniel accused her of not loving him, of hiding things, of planning to abandon him. You’d repeated those fears so often, Daniel believed them himself. Lila cried on the phone to you once, begging you to tell him she wasn’t going anywhere. You said, *“I can’t lie to him, Lila. I have to protect my son.”* But you weren’t protecting him. You were keeping him yours.

Gina saw it. She said, “Maria, you’re smothering him. He’s thirty-two. He needs to breathe.” You told Gina she didn’t understand motherhood. You said she didn’t have kids, so she couldn’t know what love like yours felt like. Gina stopped calling for six months. When she came back, she brought you cannoli. You forgave her. Or pretended to.

Daniel met Rachel two years later. She was kind, quiet, a nurse. She reminded you of yourself at twenty-five. That scared you. You told Daniel she was “too passive,” that she’d let him walk all over her. You said she wouldn’t stand up for him in a crisis. You called her dull. You said, “You can do better.” You said it every time her name came up.

Then Daniel moved in with Rachel. You didn’t speak to him for three weeks. When you finally did, you said, “I just want what’s best for you.” You cried. He came over, hugged you. You whispered, “Don’t lose me, Danny. I couldn’t survive that.”

Two months later, Daniel and Rachel were driving back from visiting Gina in Maine. It was raining. Rachel was at the wheel. Daniel argued with her about you—that you didn’t like her, that you’d been distant since the engagement. He said you were all he had. Rachel said, “She’s not going to live forever, Daniel. You need to build your own life.” He screamed. He reached for the wheel. Rachel swerved. The car hydroplaned, flipped twice, landed in a ravine.

Rachel died instantly. Daniel lived for seventeen minutes. His last words, according to the paramedic, were: “Tell my mother I’m sorry.”

You died three years later, in your sleep, of a heart attack. You never told anyone about the call from the hospital. You never admitted that you taught your son to believe love meant ownership. That you trained him to fear losing you more than anything else. That you needed him afraid of being without you.

You called it love. You still do. Even now. Especially now.

prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell to be tortured for all eternity, for a deadly sin you
committed.

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. No longer than 600 words. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 57
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
